stories.headline: US STRIKES IRAN FOR A SIXTH STRAIGHT NIGHT AS OIL JUMPS 4% AND THE DOLLAR, NOT GOLD, BECOMES THIS WEEK'S SAFE HAVEN
stories.body: US Central Command carried out a sixth consecutive night of airstrikes on Iranian military and logistics targets, sending WTI up 4.00% to $82.11 a barrel and Brent up 2.04% to $85.95, both near one-month highs, as Hormuz shipping traffic thinned and Tehran signaled the Houthis could move to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The S&P 500 fell 1.01% to 7,457.69 while investors rotated into the dollar rather than gold, with the DXY holding near 100.78.
stories.explain: Oil chokepoint risk gets priced into futures the moment a threat becomes credible, since roughly a fifth of global oil consumption transits Hormuz and rerouting options shrink further once Bab el-Mandeb is also in play - that's why crude jumped before a single extra barrel actually stopped moving. The dollar, not gold, is absorbing this week's safe-haven flows because the same oil shock that raises war risk also lifts US inflation expectations and trims bets on near-term Fed cuts, which supports a yield-bearing currency more than a zero-yield metal.

stories.headline: CHIP STOCKS SLIDE TOWARD A BEAR MARKET AS CHINA'S KIMI K3 AND A NETFLIX MISS DEEPEN THE NASDAQ SELLOFF
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.49% to about 28,592.66 as the semiconductor group extended its worst weekly rout since last year's tariff selloff, down roughly 20% from its record on doubts that AI infrastructure spending can keep justifying current valuations. Chinese startup Moonshot's new Kimi K3 model, competitive with leading US models, compounded the unease, while Netflix shares fell more than 10% after revenue of $12.56 billion narrowly missed the $12.6 billion consensus despite an EPS beat.
stories.explain: Chip stocks trade on the market's confidence that hyperscaler capex converts into durable revenue, so evidence that a Chinese competitor can match frontier AI performance for less directly threatens the pricing power baked into demand forecasts for that capex. Netflix's tiny revenue miss drew an outsized 10% punishment because at its valuation the market was pricing near-flawless execution, and a roughly $40 million shortfall against a $12.6 billion consensus was enough to break that assumption.

stories.headline: GOLD HEADS FOR ITS WORST WEEK SINCE JUNE EVEN AS IRAN AIRSTRIKES INTENSIFY
stories.body: Gold slipped to about $3,980 an ounce, down roughly 0.3% on the day and 3.4% for the week - its steepest weekly drop in six weeks - even as US strikes on Iran entered a sixth night. Silver fell alongside it to an eight-month low, with both metals losing out to the dollar as this week's preferred safe-haven trade.
stories.explain: Gold usually rallies on exactly this kind of shock, but it's losing a tug-of-war with two forces working against it: a firmer dollar pulling safe-haven flows its own direction, and oil-driven inflation expectations that make traders less confident the Fed keeps cutting, which raises the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset. When a safe-haven asset falls during a genuine geopolitical escalation, it usually means a competing asset - here, the dollar - is absorbing the flows that would otherwise go to it.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.55% AS TRADERS PRICE JUST A 12% CHANCE OF A JULY HIKE, BUT THE OIL SHOCK CLOUDS THE PATH
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped about 3 basis points to 4.55% and the 2-year eased to 4.18% after this week's cooler June CPI left futures markets pricing roughly a 12% probability of a Fed hike this month and about 56% by September. That calm is now colliding with a fresh oil shock: WTI's 4% jump on the Iran conflict threatens to reverse the disinflation narrative that pulled yields lower in the first place.
stories.explain: Cooler CPI normally pulls yields down because it raises the odds the Fed can hold or cut instead of hike, and today's move follows that script. But a sustained oil shock works through the same inflation channel in reverse - energy costs feed directly into headline CPI and into transportation costs economy-wide - so if crude's rally holds, the same data that just talked yields lower could reverse course within a month or two, which is exactly the tension the market is now pricing into the curve.

stories.headline: TEXAS LANDS NO. 1-CLASS FORWARD MARCUS SPEARS AS DUKE TOPS THE PRESEASON POWER 44 AND KANSAS VAULTS IN BEHIND TYRAN STOKES
stories.body: Six-foot-10 forward Marcus Spears reclassified into the 2026 class and picked Texas over Arizona, LSU and Kentucky, giving the Longhorns a two-way frontcourt piece that puts them in the national title conversation. Kansas vaulted into early 2026-27 rankings after landing five-star forward Tyran Stokes, the top overall recruit in the class, while Duke opened Andy Katz's first Power 44 at No. 1 amid a portal cycle that has already moved more than 2,700 players since the 2025-26 season ended.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES TELLS LAKERS HE WON'T RETURN FOR 2026-27 AS HARDEN DECLINES $42.3M CAVALIERS OPTION
stories.body: LeBron James has informed the Los Angeles Lakers he will not be back next season, with little communication between the two sides beyond initial contact, opening a free-agency chase in which Cleveland and Golden State both view themselves as contenders. Separately, Cavaliers guard James Harden declined the final $42.3 million year of his contract to negotiate a new multiyear deal with Cleveland rather than test the open market, while Phoenix's Mark Williams agreed to a three-year, $38 million deal to stay with the Suns.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS' $9.6 BILLION SALE TO KHOSLA-LED GROUP AWAITS OWNER VOTE AS SAINTS BRING BACK ALVIN KAMARA
stories.body: The Paul Allen Estate has agreed to sell the reigning Super Bowl champion Seahawks to a Khosla family-led group for a reported $9.612 billion, a deal that still needs ratification from at least 24 of the other 31 NFL owners. Elsewhere, Alvin Kamara returned to New Orleans on a pay cut after the Saints signed Travis Etienne Jr., and Commissioner Roger Goodell said the league is eyeing roughly 10 additional countries - including Japan - as it pushes to expand international games to 16 per year.

stories.headline: TEXAS ADDS AUBURN'S CAM COLEMAN TO SURROUND ARCH MANNING AS THE TRANSFER PORTAL CYCLE TOPS 3,600 PLAYERS
stories.body: Texas landed wide receiver Cam Coleman from Auburn, who piled up 1,306 yards and 13 touchdowns over the past two seasons, giving Arch Manning another explosive target ahead of fall camp. The 2026 cycle - the first without a spring transfer window - has now seen 3,664 of 14,070 FBS players enter the portal, with Ohio State's pull of Alabama lineman James Smith and Texas A&M's addition of receiver Isaiah Horton among the other moves reshaping the sport's top tier.

sports.detail: No game until the Apple Cup opener vs. Washington State, now moved to Sunday, Sept. 6 (1 p.m. PT, NBC). Jedd Fisch's staff added a 4-star cornerback, its highest-rated 2026 commitment, along with Censere Gaylord, as it builds toward year two in Seattle.

Forward Hannes Steinbach was taken 14th overall by the Charlotte Hornets in the 2026 NBA Draft. Danny Sprinkle's staff is rebuilding around a heavy international pipeline after landing Croatian forward Boris Tisma, with Jasir Rencher looking healthy - shooting, driving and lifting - in offseason workouts.

Fresh off their Super Bowl LX title, the Seahawks open training camp July 25 in Renton with nine public practices and an HBO Hard Knocks feature this fall. RB Zach Charbonnet is progressing well in his ACL rehab ahead of a late-July checkup, and the club's $9.6B sale to a Khosla-led group now awaits ratification from at least 24 of the other 31 owners.

Fresh off a 60-22, No. 1-seed finish in the East, Detroit (1-3 in Summer League) closes out Las Vegas today against Miami (also 1-3) in the consolation finale - Detroit's last result was a 100-88 loss to Phoenix on July 15. The Pistons also agreed to a three-year, $51M deal with forward John Collins and landed Jrue Holiday in a trade with Milwaukee this offseason.
Seattle sits 2nd in the AL West behind Texas and holds a wild-card spot. The Mariners host the Giants (41-55) tonight at T-Mobile Park, first pitch 7:10 p.m. PT (10:10 p.m. ET).

deepDive.title: When the Safe Haven Isn't Gold: How the Dollar Displaced Gold During Today's Iran Escalation
content: Today handed markets a textbook geopolitical shock - a sixth straight night of US airstrikes on Iran, oil up 4%, stocks lower - and gold did the opposite of what the textbook predicts. Instead of rallying on safe-haven demand, gold slipped about 0.3% on the day and is now down 3.4% for the week, its worst stretch in six weeks, even as silver fell to an eight-month low alongside it. Meanwhile the dollar index held firm near 100.78. That divergence is the interesting part: two assets that are both supposed to catch a bid when geopolitical risk rises, and only one of them did.

The mechanism is a competition for the same flow of frightened capital. When investors want safety, they can buy gold, Treasuries, or dollars, and today the dollar won that competition for two reasons. First, the same oil spike that signals war risk also signals higher near-term inflation, which makes traders less confident the Fed will keep cutting rates - and a currency backed by higher-for-longer rates draws its own demand independent of the war headlines. Second, gold pays no yield, so every basis point that stays elevated on the 10-year raises the opportunity cost of holding it instead of interest-bearing dollar assets, even while the geopolitical case for owning gold is getting stronger by the day.

This is not a new pattern, but it's easy to forget because gold's headline reputation as "the" safe haven obscures how often the dollar wins this exact contest. During the 1990 Gulf War buildup, gold rallied - but so did the dollar, and by more, as investors defaulted to the world's reserve currency first. The more instructive lesson is that gold's safe-haven premium is conditional: it shows up cleanly when real yields are falling and the dollar is already weak, and it gets crowded out precisely when a shock also pushes yields or the dollar higher at the same time, which is exactly today's setup.

For anyone watching this market, the read-through is to stop treating oil headlines as a standalone gold signal and start watching the DXY and real (inflation-adjusted) yields alongside them. If the Iran conflict keeps oil elevated long enough to genuinely lift inflation expectations, the Fed's rate path becomes the swing factor: a Fed that holds rates higher for longer to fight oil-driven inflation keeps gold's opportunity cost elevated even as the war itself intensifies. Gold's real signal to buy, in that scenario, arrives only once the market decides the Fed will look through the oil shock - not when the strikes escalate.
